issues.legal_issue: A housing authority may not impose an excessive increase in the price of allotted houses contrary to the scheme’s stated price limit when the authority caused the unjustified delay in allotment and possession.
material_facts: The applicants applied within time, met the scheme’s conditions, and were not parties to the suits that delayed the authority’s actions.
The scheme stated an estimated house price, allowed an increase of no more than 10%, and provided that the final price would be determined when construction was completed.
The houses were completed in 1980, but the authority did not allot them to the applicants then, although houses were available in excess of the valid applications.
The authority determined the price in 1994 at nearly four and a half times the estimated price, and required the applicants to pay the increased amount.
The delay was attributable to the authority, and it provided no adequate particulars or material to justify the increase by reference to its loan interest or other costs.
issues.conclusion: The appeals were dismissed, leaving in force the order quashing the increased price and directing delivery of the houses at the price fixed in the scheme brochure.
issues.legal_principle: Price escalation by a development authority must be assessed on the facts and under the scheme and application terms. Where the scheme fixes a limit, the price ordinarily cannot exceed it; any escalation must be supported by material and cannot be arbitrary or erratic. The cause of delay and any unforeseen reasons beyond the authority’s control are relevant. In Indore Development Authority v. Sadhana Agarwal, the Court recognized the authority’s duty to explain substantial escalation, while noting that a reviewing court need not examine every construction detail. Delhi Development Authority v. Pushpendra Kumar Jain held that selection by lottery alone does not create a right to the price prevailing on the draw date, but was distinguished because the scheme there permitted revision and the delay was not unreasonable. Bareilly Development Authority v. Ajai Pal Singh was discussed concerning changed scheme terms and accepted variations. Prashant Kumar Shahi v. Ghaziabad Development Authority supports the principle that an allottee should not bear interest attributable to the authority’s delay. No statutory provision was relied on to decide this price issue.

rule.if: housing_allotment_appeal and applicants_met_scheme_conditions and scheme_capped_escalation and final_price_due_at_completion and authority_caused_unjustified_delay and authority_imposed_excessive_increase and not authority_supported_increase

predicates.housing_allotment_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning the price charged for houses allotted under a housing scheme.
predicates.applicants_met_scheme_conditions: The applicants complied with the scheme’s application and payment conditions.
predicates.scheme_capped_escalation: The scheme stated a limit on how much the estimated price could increase.
predicates.final_price_due_at_completion: The scheme provided that the final price would be determined when construction was completed.
predicates.authority_caused_unjustified_delay: The authority, rather than the applicants, caused an unjustified delay in allotment or delivery of possession.
predicates.authority_imposed_excessive_increase: The authority imposed a price increase that substantially exceeded the scheme’s stated estimate or limit.
predicates.authority_supported_increase: The authority placed adequate material on record to justify the increase.

issues.definition: When applicants comply with a housing scheme that limits price escalation and fixes the final price at construction completion, an authority-caused unjustified delay does not permit an unsupported excessive increase.

issues.legal_issue: A court need not order an inquiry into alleged false or fabricated evidence when it considers further investigation unnecessary to resolve the proceedings before it.
material_facts: The applicants sought an inquiry and prosecution concerning the authority’s alleged use of a false or fabricated translation of the scheme brochure in judicial proceedings.
The original brochure in the relevant language was produced, and the authority’s counsel did not dispute its correctness or authenticity.
The Court resolved the appeals on their merits and stated that it was unnecessary to probe the allegations further in those proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The Court made no order on the applications seeking an inquiry.
issues.legal_principle: The Court did not decide whether an offence had been committed or state a general test for ordering an inquiry. It concluded only that further investigation into the allegations was unnecessary in these proceedings because the appeals could be disposed of on their merits. The applications invoked Sections 340 and 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and provisions of the Indian Penal Code, but the Court made no determination under those provisions.

predicates.ancillary_inquiry_application: A party made an application within the proceeding seeking an inquiry into alleged misconduct in judicial proceedings.
predicates.alleged_false_evidence: The applicant alleged that another participant submitted false or fabricated material or gave false evidence.
predicates.court_can_resolve_main_proceeding_withou: The court resolved the main proceeding without needing to investigate the allegation.

issues.definition: When a party seeks an inquiry into alleged false evidence but the court can resolve the main proceeding without that inquiry, the court may make no inquiry order.
